bounded_inventory.content: The ambient space is real Euclidean R^n. Throughout the book n is a fixed positive integer greater than 1, and Omega is an open nonempty subset of R^n. The scalar function u is complex-valued. On an open set, harmonic means twice continuously differentiable with Delta u = 0, where Delta = sum_j D_j^2. The norm is the ordinary Euclidean norm. The coordinate functions and the displayed complex-valued R^3 example illustrate these conventions.
bounded_inventory.boundary: No n=1 case or infinite-dimensional ambient space is included in this source convention. Real-valued functions are a specialization of the complex-valued source setting.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 1 / PDF 9, paragraph defining harmonicity on E
bounded_inventory.content: For a function defined on E contained in R^n, with E not necessarily open, harmonic on E means that the function has an extension harmonic on some open set containing E.
bounded_inventory.closed_ball_consequence: Harmonic on the closed ball means a harmonic extension to an open neighborhood of that entire closed ball. The extension supplies C^2 regularity and harmonicity across the boundary and throughout the filled ball; the phrase is not merely harmonicity on the open ball plus a separate continuous boundary trace.
bounded_inventory.boundary: No global extension to all of R^n is required.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 4 / PDF 12, equation 1.1 and its following paragraph
bounded_inventory.formula: integral_Omega (u Delta v - v Delta u) dV = integral_boundary(Omega) (u D_n v - v D_n u) ds
bounded_inventory.conditions: Omega is bounded and open in R^n with smooth boundary; u and v are C^2 on a neighborhood of closure(Omega). V = V_n is Lebesgue volume measure on R^n. The boundary measure s is surface-area measure. The derivative D_n is differentiation along the outward unit normal, not a coordinate derivative indexed by the integer n.
bounded_inventory.normal_formula: (D_n u)(zeta) = grad u(zeta) dot n(zeta), with grad u = (D_1 u,...,D_n u).
bounded_inventory.scalar_convention: The source has complex-valued scalar functions and displays products without conjugation. Pairing a complex gradient with the real outward normal is componentwise sum_j (D_j u) n_j; no conjugation of u or v appears in Green's identity.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 4 / PDF 12, equation 1.2 and following paragraph
bounded_inventory.formula: integral_Omega div w dV = integral_boundary(Omega) w dot n ds
bounded_inventory.conditions: The same domain context is in force. The vector field w = (w_1,...,w_n) takes values in C^n and has continuously differentiable components on a neighborhood of closure(Omega). The source calls this a smooth vector field and defines div w = sum_j D_j w_j.
bounded_inventory.source_dependency: The familiar divergence theorem of advanced calculus is invoked, not proved in these pages. Green's identity is obtained by setting w = u grad v - v grad u and computing its divergence.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 4 / PDF 12, equation 1.3 and its preceding sentence
bounded_inventory.content: The source obtains this useful form of Green's identity when u is harmonic and v is identically 1, in the preceding bounded smooth-domain and neighborhood-regularity context.
bounded_inventory.dependency_chain: Divergence theorem 1.2 -> Green identity 1.1 using w = u grad v - v grad u -> zero flux 1.3 using v = 1 and Delta u = 0.
bounded_inventory.boundary: The source does not state zero flux for a function harmonic only on a punctured region when the displayed sphere encloses a singularity.

bounded_inventory.content: B(a,r) = {x in R^n : |x-a| < r}; its closure is the closed ball. B = B(0,1), closure(B) is the closed unit ball, and B_n is used when ambient dimension matters. S is boundary(B). The measure sigma on S is normalized surface-area measure with sigma(S) = 1; it is identified as the unique rotation-invariant Borel probability measure, where invariance is under every orthogonal transformation.
bounded_inventory.radius_scope: The source uses ordinary ball/radius terminology and normalizes to the unit ball. A positive radius is implicit in that nondegenerate normalization; the displayed 1.4 sentence does not separately print an r > 0 binder.
bounded_inventory.measure_distinction: The ds in Green/divergence/zero-flux displays is unnormalized area; d sigma in the mean-value display is normalized unit-sphere probability measure.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 5 / PDF 13, 1.4 and first proof paragraph
bounded_inventory.source_statement: For u harmonic on the closed ball centered at a of radius r, u(a) is the normalized spherical average integral_S u(a+r zeta) d sigma(zeta).
bounded_inventory.source_route: First take n > 2, reduce without loss of generality to the closed unit ball, fix epsilon in (0,1), and apply Green 1.1 to A_epsilon = {x : epsilon < |x| < 1} with v(x) = |x|^(2-n).
bounded_inventory.regularity_scope: The singular auxiliary v is used only on the annulus and its neighborhood avoiding 0. The harmonic extension of u on the closed unit ball also covers the two filled balls used in the subsequent cancellations.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 5 / PDF 13, first display in the proof of 1.4
bounded_inventory.normals: On outer S, the annulus outward unit normal is x. On inner epsilon S, the annulus outward unit normal is -x/epsilon. The outward normal of the filled epsilon ball is instead +x/epsilon.
bounded_inventory.source_display: 0 = (2-n) integral_S u ds - (2-n) epsilon^(1-n) integral_(epsilon S) u ds - integral_S D_n u ds - epsilon^(2-n) integral_(epsilon S) D_n u ds
bounded_inventory.reading_of_inner_derivative: The D_n in the annular boundary formula uses the annulus outward normal; at the inner sphere it therefore has the opposite sign to the filled inner ball's normal derivative. This accounts for the displayed minus sign in front of the inner flux term.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 5 / PDF 13, sentence 'By 1.3' following the annular display, read with printed 1 and 4
bounded_inventory.content: One use of 1.3 is on the filled outer unit ball B. The harmonic extension of u covers closure(B). The outward normal on S agrees with the outer annulus normal, so integral_S D_n u ds = 0 with that orientation.
bounded_inventory.separate_obligation: This is an individual outer-boundary flux cancellation. It is not obtained merely by knowing the sum of fluxes on the two annular boundary components is zero.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 5 / PDF 13, the same 'By 1.3' sentence, read with printed 1 and 4
bounded_inventory.content: A distinct use of 1.3 is on the filled ball {x : |x| < epsilon}. Harmonicity and C^2 regularity extend through its center and across its spherical boundary. The flux for this filled ball's outward normal is zero. Reversing that normal negates the flux and therefore also gives zero for the inner annulus normal.
bounded_inventory.separate_obligation: This cancellation needs harmonicity on the filled inner ball. Annular harmonicity alone does not provide it. The singular v(x) = |x|^(2-n) is not the function to which zero flux is applied on the filled inner ball; the function is u, with the constant test function from 1.3.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 5 / PDF 13, remainder of the proof of 1.4
bounded_inventory.content: After the two flux terms vanish and n > 2 allows cancellation of 2-n, the source obtains integral_S u ds = epsilon^(1-n) integral_(epsilon S) u ds. It rewrites this as integral_S u d sigma = integral_S u(epsilon zeta) d sigma(zeta), then lets epsilon tend to 0 using continuity at 0. For n = 2 the source says to use log|x| in place of |x|^(2-n).
bounded_inventory.scope_notes: The n = 2 logarithmic route is a separate dimension case, not substitution of n = 2 into a division by 2-n. Both filled-ball zero-flux facts remain available in that case, though log(1) makes the outer flux coefficient zero. The text does not discuss n = 1.

bounded_inventory.anchor: printed 240 / PDF 242, surface-area paragraph and footnote
bounded_inventory.content: S_n denotes the unit sphere living in R^n. The footnote contrasts the more common S^(n-1), which emphasizes manifold dimension n-1. The appendix denotes unnormalized surface-area measure by s_n and normalized surface-area measure by sigma_n.
bounded_inventory.context: The paragraph explicitly says that some remaining appendix arguments are more intuitive than rigorous and presumes familiarity with surface-area measure. The page then gives the thin-shell calculus argument leading to A.2: s_n(S_n) = n V_n(B_n).
bounded_inventory.boundary: The notation does not mean an n-dimensional manifold sphere. This page is not a complete rigorous construction of surface measure or of all surface change-of-variables formulas. No identification with a particular formal library measure normalization has been inspected.

details_left_implicit_or_external_in_the.detail: The general divergence theorem is an external advanced-calculus input. The product-rule cancellation yielding div(u grad v - v grad u) = u Delta v - v Delta u is delegated to 'compute'.

details_left_implicit_or_external_in_the.topic: extension witness and admissible filled balls
details_left_implicit_or_external_in_the.detail: The closed-set harmonic convention supplies an open harmonic extension. Using it on both filled balls, checking their closures lie in its domain, and recognizing each sphere as the smooth boundary of its filled ball are not expanded in the mean-value proof.

The single sentence citing 1.3 suppresses two separate filled-domain invocations and the sign reversal of the inner boundary normal. Applying 1.3 only to the annulus would give a relation between component fluxes, not their separate vanishing.

The harmonicity and radial derivatives of |x|^(2-n) away from 0, the two boundary components, and their opposite orientations are used without a detailed calculation. For n = 2 the corresponding log|x| calculation is only indicated.

Translation/dilation to the unit ball, surface-area scaling by epsilon^(n-1), and passage from ds to normalized d sigma are compressed source steps. A formal measure comparison needs its exact scale and normalization, not just an appeal to an unspecified sphere integral.

The source only says to use continuity at 0 as epsilon tends to 0. Since |epsilon zeta| = epsilon on S and sigma is a probability measure, the needed uniform smallness of u(epsilon zeta)-u(0) follows from that continuity. Compact smooth boundaries and neighborhood regularity also supply ordinary finite surface integrals; these analytic details are not separate printed premises.
